title: Reading versus ad-lib playing; the new Edith Wilson record
summary: He feels freer playing without music, though he reads, and mentions his recent session behind Edith Wilson and subbing in theater bands.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you first started playing, were you playing with Bantam, you were all playing your arrangements? The first band that you played with, was Bernie and John?
With Bernie, what you asked me about, Bernie?
When you made those recordings like in 1923, 24, were you using arrangements with those bands? No, no arrangements.

Then you were at living on the one? Yeah, at living, that's right. And I've always felt more freely at living than when I'm reading the music. You see now this recording we made just a few days ago, we had this skeleton arrangements, you know, behind Edith Wilson, the old singer Edith Wilson. Well we had, she had a background, we just caused, you know? And then spots where certain guys take solos. Now I recorded two of my own tunes. I sang on this, which I'm not much of a singer, but I think it may pass on Goodbye Mr. Blues. And I had another tune, I called it Dilsa's Blues. And so we recorded both of those. Do you have the music to those numbers?
Huh? Do you have a lead sheet to those numbers?
I have a lead sheet to them, yeah. I just sent a, I can.
You might want to tell the player. Huh?

Well I can, I might can obtain it from you, for you rather, from Leon Scotty. Leon Scotty, we called him Scotty, his name is Scott Leon Scotty, the trumpet player, because he made me a lead sheet. And I had, I gave Brother Montgomery the money, to send the money in to have it copyrighted, you know? And so I'll write to him right away. I'll write tonight or this afternoon and tell him to make me up a lead sheet. Now he may charge two or three dollars for that, you understand? But he will do it for me. He's a nice trumpet player too. So that's my story. I mean I'm still, yeah I start out that way. But I could read. But I could read music.
Then you became, even when you played with all those bigger band reading matches, you still play ad-libs?

Yeah well I'm not bragging but this is the category I was in. Whenever a band came to Rega Theater short of a trombone player, they used to look at me. There was Bo Moose Johnson or something like that. Jackson. Jackson. And there was Ella Fitzgerald. I played about five or six different bands, you know, short of trombone player. And they sent for me. And there wasn't a rehearsal, you understand? Jimmy Newman sent for me. They put the music on. I was able to play it, you understand what I'm talking about? Okay. Boy, it's living good, taking care of today.
